q: Which row describes a typical metal?
explain: Metals conduct heat well, usually have high melting points and are malleable, unlike most non-metals.

q: What does it mean when a metal is described as ductile?
options: It can be hammered into thin sheets
It can be drawn out into wires
It makes a ringing sound when struck
explain: Ductile means a material can be stretched into wire; being hammered into sheets is malleability.

q: A solid conducts electricity and can be bent without breaking. What is it most likely to be?
explain: Metals conduct as solids and are malleable, whereas sulfur, ionic solids and simple covalent solids do not conduct and are brittle or crumbly.

q: Which products form when a metal such as zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
explain: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace hydrogen from acids, giving a salt and hydrogen gas.

q: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which gas is given off and how is it identified?
options: Hydrogen, which relights a glowing splint
Hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop
Oxygen, which burns with a squeaky pop
Chlorine, which bleaches damp litmus paper
explain: The gas is hydrogen, and a lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube makes a squeaky pop.

q: Which type of oxide do most metals form when they react with oxygen?
explain: Metal oxides are basic (they react with acids to form salts), while many non-metal oxides are acidic.

q: Calcium reacts with cold water. Which pair of products forms?
explain: A reactive metal and cold water give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

q: Magnesium ribbon is heated in air until it ignites. Which observation is correct?
options: An orange flame and a black solid
A blue flame and a colourless gas
A bright white flame and a white solid
A red flame and a green solid
explain: Magnesium burns with a bright white flame to form white magnesium oxide, MgO.

q: Which statement about metals is correct?
options: Most are liquids at room temperature
Most have lower melting points than non-metals
Most are solids at room temperature with high melting points
explain: Only mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature, and most metals have high melting and boiling points.

q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
options: Positive ions move through the structure
Electrons are held in fixed positions between atoms
Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice
Mobile negative ions carry the charge
explain: In a metal the outer electrons are delocalised and move, carrying charge; the positive ions stay in fixed positions.

q: A student tests four solids. Which result is the best evidence that solid X is a metal?
options: It conducts electricity when solid and is malleable
It has a low melting point and does not conduct
It conducts electricity only when molten
explain: Conduction as a solid together with malleability is typical of metals; ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved.

q: Which statement about non-metals is correct?
options: Most solid non-metals are brittle and poor conductors of heat
Most solid non-metals are malleable and ductile
Most solid non-metals conduct electricity well
explain: Non-metals are generally brittle as solids and poor thermal and electrical conductors; graphite is an exception.

q: 0.24 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess dilute sulfuric acid. What volume of hydrogen forms at room temperature and pressure? (Ar: Mg = 24; 1 mol of gas = 24 000 cm³)
explain: Moles of Mg = 0.24 ÷ 24 = 0.010 mol; Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂ gives 0.010 mol H₂, which is 0.010 × 24 000 = 240 cm³.

q: Which is a chemical property of metals rather than a physical property?
explain: Reacting with acids changes the metal into a new substance, so it is chemical; the others describe physical behaviour.

q: Which property of aluminium makes it suitable for the body of an aircraft?
explain: A low density keeps the aircraft light so less fuel is needed.

q: Which pair of properties makes aluminium suitable for overhead electrical cables?
options: Low density and good electrical conductivity
High density and good electrical conductivity
Low density and poor electrical conductivity
High density and poor electrical conductivity
explain: The cables must carry current and also be light enough to be supported between pylons.

q: Why is aluminium used to make food containers?
options: It has a very high melting point
explain: Aluminium does not corrode easily, so the container and the food stay in good condition.

q: Which row correctly matches a metal, a use and the property that makes it suitable?
options: Copper | electrical wiring | ductile and a good conductor
explain: Copper can be drawn into wires and conducts electricity well, so it is used in wiring.

q: Copper wires in a household cable are covered with plastic. Why?
options: Plastic conducts electricity better than copper
Plastic reacts with the copper to make it stronger
explain: The plastic insulates the wire so people are not shocked and current stays in the copper.

q: Which property of copper makes it suitable for the base of a cooking pan?
options: It is a good electrical insulator
It is a good conductor of heat
explain: Heat must pass quickly from the cooker through the base into the food.

q: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium food containers hardly corrode. Why?
options: Aluminium is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
A thin layer of aluminium oxide on the surface protects the metal
Aluminium does not react with oxygen
Manufacturers always coat it with zinc
explain: Aluminium reacts quickly with oxygen to form an unreactive oxide layer that stops further reaction.

q: Why are aluminium cables preferred to copper cables on long overhead power lines?
options: Aluminium is a better electrical conductor than copper
Aluminium has a higher density so the cables are stronger
Aluminium has a lower density so the cables are lighter
Aluminium is magnetic and stays on the pylon
explain: Aluminium conducts well enough and is much less dense than copper, so the cables put less load on the pylons.

q: Which property of metals allows steel to be pressed into car body panels?
explain: Malleable metals can be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.

q: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g/cm³ and of copper is 9.0 g/cm³. How much less mass does 1000 cm³ of aluminium have than 1000 cm³ of copper?
explain: Mass = density × volume: copper 9.0 × 1000 = 9000 g, aluminium 2.7 × 1000 = 2700 g, so the difference is 6300 g.

q: Which property of copper allows it to be pulled into long thin wires?
explain: Ductile metals can be drawn out into wire.

q: Which statement about aluminium is correct?
options: It has a high density and is a poor conductor
It has a low density and conducts electricity well
explain: These properties explain its use in aircraft and overhead cables.

q: What is an alloy?
options: A mixture of a metal with other elements
A pure metal with a coating
explain: An alloy is a mixture, not a compound, and contains at least one metal.

q: Which two metals are mixed to make brass?
explain: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; copper and tin make bronze.

q: Which elements are mixed with iron in stainless steel?
explain: Stainless steel is iron with other elements such as chromium, nickel and carbon.

q: Stainless steel is used for cutlery. Which properties make it suitable?
options: It is hard and resists rusting
It is soft and easily shaped
It is a good conductor of electricity
It has a very low density
explain: Cutlery must stay hard and must not rust when washed and used with food.
